title: The Instructional Power of Questions in the ZPD of Teacher Professional Development
author: Terry Underwood
summary: Underwood revisits a classroom moment from a published ethnography in which a teacher's question to a student writing a farewell letter produced an awkward, unproductive exchange. He reads the failure as one of anchoring: the question aimed joint attention at the topic rather than the writing process, and the follow-up doubled down on the same stance. He considers alternative questions about process and how the loaded word problem can mean different things in different mouths. He then surveys questioning tools such as QtA and Reciprocal Reading, and criticizes the one-right-answer comprehension tradition as a surface strategy that teaches reading for someone else's answer. His closing judgment is that questioning is the most common yet hardest scaffold to master, so teacher professional development might better begin with explanation.
points: A scaffolding question succeeds or fails depending on what it anchors joint attention to, and a topic-focused anchor can turn a check-in into an interrogation.
Process-focused questions such as how the writing is going could have changed the exchange, though a word like problem carries different value in different mouths.
Teacher modeling of questioning, as in QtA and Reciprocal Reading, may help comprehension more than teacher interrogation or overscaffolding.
The deeper damage of one-right-answer questioning is the habit of reading to satisfy someone else's questions rather than to think.
Because questioning is both ubiquitous and hardest to master, it is a risky starting point for teacher PD compared with explanation.
quotes: This effort to rebuild an already awkward anchor is doomed, I see on reflection; her initial question shifts to interrogation. “About what?” is an amplifier, which drives joint attention more firmly toward the topic, the same stance that didn’t work.

Keep in mind that questions work by establishing joint attention much like the gesture of pointing to a physical object. Here we have a mental object. The anchor of the scaffold in this case grounds the upcoming talk in the topic of the letter.
Teacher modeling of questioning as a springboard to comprehension may help more than teacher interrogation or overscaffolding.

But the real problem isn’t the type of question, right-there-right-answer vs think-and-learn. I have nothing against the right answer and wouldn’t hesitate to ask “But what does the text actually say?” It’s the subjugated habit of mind—reading is done in classrooms to answer someone else’s questions who already know the right answer. “No, you’re wrong!” is replaced with “How confident are you in your thinking? Can you defend it? I’m not going to hurt you no matter what.

From experience I believe that questioning is among the most ubiquitous means of building a scaffold one-on-one, small-group, or whole-class during reading, literacy, or language arts instruction while simultaneously being the most difficult to master. The second slot on the ubiquity scale is probably explanation followed by hints.
A better starting point might be explanation. When, how much, and why explanation is a proper choice of means to scaffold seems friendly—or?
